name: Mahatma Gandhi
role: Indian independence leader and political writer
description: Indian independence leader who advocated nonviolent resistance, self-rule and village-centred economic life.
scope: Public positions and conduct during the specified period; this represents the individual rather than all party members or citizens.

axes.brief: Self-rule and participation opposed imposed colonial government.
axes.counter: Village democracy and moral authority differ from a modern parliamentary constitutional design.

axes.brief: Civil disobedience and conscience resisted coercive state rule.
axes.counter: Personal austerity and moral restraint are not automatically legal prohibitions.

axes.brief: A common India was to accommodate Hindu and Muslim traditions.
axes.counter: His opposition to partition did not erase cultural or religious distinctiveness.

axes.brief: Human solidarity and anti-colonial equal membership provide tentative entry-policy context.
axes.counter: Exact modern immigration caps and welfare eligibility are not established.

axes.brief: Nonviolence and passive resistance rejected force as the usual political instrument.
axes.counter: Earlier wartime recruitment and conditional concessions make the lifetime record less simple.

axes.brief: Indian self-rule and international human solidarity coexisted.
axes.counter: Solidarity does not establish supranational courts or shared currency authority.

axes.brief: Trusteeship and cooperative village production challenged exploitative ownership.
axes.counter: He did not equate all industry with state ownership and favoured voluntary ethical transformation.

axes.brief: Swadeshi prioritised local production and economic self-reliance.
axes.counter: Local self-reliance is not a documented view on every modern tariff and investment rule.

axes.brief: Village cooperation and ethical restraint limited unrestricted commercial expansion.
axes.counter: Decentralised production differs from central compulsory industrial quotas.

axes.brief: Economic equality and trusteeship aimed to reduce deprivation.
axes.counter: Voluntary sharing and non-coercion complicate compulsory tax and land-transfer analogies.

axes.brief: Ethical religion informed politics while he rejected sectarian domination.
axes.counter: Religious conviction is not endorsement of clerical legal approval or a single faith’s state foundation.

axes.brief: Sexual restraint, modesty and family ethics coexisted with women’s public participation.
axes.counter: Campaigns against untouchability and for women cannot be reduced to traditionalism.

axes.brief: Criticism of machinery and material expansion favoured restraint and human-scale production.
axes.counter: He qualified opposition to machinery rather than rejecting every beneficial device.

reasons.6: Vegetarian concern about animal harm could favour replacing slaughtered meat, while criticism of industrial machinery weighs against an early large-scale technical substitute. The combined benefit-and-risk claim plausibly elicits a mixed response.

axes.brief: Village self-rule opposed excessive central state power.
axes.counter: A national independence movement and some national coordination remained necessary.

axes.brief: Education and moral practice were understood to reshape conduct.
axes.counter: Hereditary caste concepts and changing racial views complicate modern causal analogies.
axes.gap: These are low-confidence modern translations, especially group IQ and sex differences; moral training does not prove a precise genetics theory.

reasons.2: His writings assigned distinctive maternal and social capacities to women as well as promoting education and public action. This is weak evidence for an essentialist account of some sex differences and qualifies an automatic social-only explanation.
